content.text:
Yes on both counts. The printer connection layer does report loaded filament — material type, color, and a filament preset ID — per slot, and the code treats those as a separate source of truth from the slicing settings, with explicit comparison and mismatch warnings between the two.

## Where the printer's filament data lives

`DevAmsTray` in [DevFilaSystem.h:66](src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceCore/DevFilaSystem.h#L66) is the per-slot record the printer fills in. The relevant fields:

- `m_fila_type` — material type string reported by the printer ("PLA", "ABS", "PETG")
- `color` — hex RGB (or RGBA) without the `#`, plus `cols` for multi-color/gradient spools and `ctype` for the color-type flag
- `setting_id` / `filament_setting_id` — the printer's own filament preset identifier
- `tag_uid` — RFID spool tag ID
- plus `nozzle_temp_min/max`, `bed_temp`, `weight`, `diameter`, `remain` (0–100 %), and per-slot calibration `k`/`n`
- `is_exists` — whether anything is actually loaded in that slot

This is populated straight from printer messages, not from any project config. For Bambu-style printers it comes over MQTT and is parsed in `DevFilaSystemParser` — see the `tray_type`, `tray_color`, `tray_info_idx`, `tray_sub_brands`, and `cols` reads at [DevFilaSystem.cpp:512-602](src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceCore/DevFilaSystem.cpp#L512).

## Two ways it's fetched

The agent interface declares a `FilamentSyncMode` in [IPrinterAgent.hpp:44](src/slic3r/Utils/IPrinterAgent.hpp#L44):

- `subscription` — pushed continuously (Bambu MQTT, via `BBLPrinterAgent`)
- `pull` — fetched on demand over REST when the UI asks. `MoonrakerPrinterAgent::fetch_filament_info()` does this and normalizes the result into its own `AmsTrayData` struct (`tray_type`, `tray_color`, `tray_info_idx`, temps) before feeding the same parser. Qidi, Creality, and Snapmaker agents subclass it and override the fetch.
- `none` — the default for agents that can't report filament at all.

There's a third, separate path for FlashForge over the generic PrintHost interface: `Flashforge::fetch_material_slots()` returns `FlashforgeMaterialSlot { slot_id, has_filament, material_name, material_color }` ([Flashforge.hpp:16](src/slic3r/Utils/Flashforge.hpp#L16)).

## Yes, they can differ — the code is built around that

The slicing side has its own parallel struct, `FilamentInfo` in [ProjectTask.hpp:38](src/libslic3r/ProjectTask.hpp#L38), with its own `type`, `color`, and `filament_id`, filled from the plate's slice results. Nothing forces the two to agree. The reconciliation happens in three places:

**1. Matching, in `DevMappingUtil::ams_filament_mapping()`** ([DevMapping.cpp:210-238](src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceCore/DevMapping.cpp#L210)). For every (sliced filament × printer slot) pair it computes a perceptual color distance and a type-equality flag:

```cpp
val.distance = GUI::calc_color_distance(c, tray_c);
if (filaments[i].type != tray->second.type) {
    val.distance = 999999;
    val.is_type_match = false;
}
```

A type mismatch is scored as effectively infinite distance, so it never auto-matches; alpha (transparency) mismatch is treated the same way. Results carry a `mapping_result` of `MAPPING_RESULT_DEFAULT`, `MAPPING_RESULT_TYPE_MISMATCH`, or `MAPPING_RESULT_EXCEED`, and slots past a distance threshold (6000) are rejected.

**2. Warnings at send time.** [SelectMachine.cpp:3519](src/slic3r/GUI/SelectMachine.cpp#L3519) compares the external-spool slot's type against the sliced filament's type and raises `PrintStatusWarningExtFilamentNotMatch`. The user-facing text lives in [PrePrintChecker.cpp:96](src/slic3r/GUI/PrePrintChecker.cpp#L96): the external filament type is unknown or doesn't match the slicing file. The AMS mapping popup has an equivalent per-slot warning at [AmsMappingPopup.cpp:1586](src/slic3r/GUI/AmsMappingPopup.cpp#L1586).

**3. Explicit sync as a user action.** `Sidebar::build_filament_ams_list()` ([Plater.cpp:3336](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp#L3336)) converts each printer slot into a `DynamicPrintConfig` carrying `filament_id`, `filament_type`, `filament_colour`, `filament_multi_colour`, `tag_uid`, `ams_id`/`slot_id`, and `filament_exist`. That list is stashed on `PresetBundle::filament_ams_list` and shown in the filament combo boxes as *available on the printer*, deliberately kept apart from the selected filament presets. Pushing printer values into the project presets only happens when the user hits sync — `Sidebar::sync_ams_list()` ([Plater.cpp:3500](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp#L3500)) opens `SyncAmsInfoDialog` for confirmation first.

## One caveat on type fidelity

The reported type isn't taken verbatim in the Bambu path. [DevFilaSystem.cpp:516](src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceCore/DevFilaSystem.cpp#L516) runs it through `MachineObject::setting_id_to_type(setting_id, tray_type)`, which prefers the type implied by the preset ID over the raw `tray_type` string. So for a slot whose RFID gives a known preset, the "printer-reported type" is partly derived from the local profile database rather than being purely what the hardware said. For third-party spools with no preset ID, the raw string is what you get, and it may be blank.

I sent three screenshots. Here's what they show and how you'd reproduce this yourself.

## The catch that shapes every answer below

The AMS mapping UI with the mismatch warnings — the one in `SelectMachine.cpp` and `AmsMappingPopup.cpp` — is gated on the printer being a Bambu Lab profile. `Plater::priv::on_action_print_plate` ([Plater.cpp:10254](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp#L10254)) only opens `SelectMachineDialog` when `preset_bundle.use_bbl_network()` is true, and that resolves to `is_bbl_vendor() && !bbl_use_printhost` ([PresetBundle.cpp:646](src/libslic3r/PresetBundle.cpp#L646)). Anything else falls through to `send_gcode_legacy` and the generic print-host dialogs. So there is no way to see *that specific* UX without a Bambu printer profile selected and a reachable Bambu device.

## What the current UX looks like

The clearest of the three is from [OrcaSlicer issue #12554](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/issues/12554): the plate was sliced in TPU, every AMS slot holds PETG. The result is a "TPU" chip in the Filament section of the Send-print-job dialog with a red exclamation badge instead of a slot assignment, an orange line reading roughly "Not all filaments … printer. Please check the mapping of filaments," a greyed-out Send button, and a picker popup ("Please select from the following filaments") that lists A1–A4 / B1–B4 as PETG. Nothing is auto-assigned, because a type mismatch scores 999999 distance and never auto-matches.

The two from [issue #13103](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/issues/13103) show the same widget on a printer with no AMS: a red "!" on the PLA chip, and a popup offering only an "External" slot rendered as a checkerboard with a "?" — that's `is_exists == false`, meaning the printer reported the external spool as empty or unknown. The wider shot shows the whole dialog for scale.

So the pattern is consistent: mismatch is never an error dialog, it's a badge plus a blocked Send, and the user resolves it by hand-picking a slot.

## Testing it, best fidelity first

**A real Bambu printer in LAN mode.** No cloud account needed. Load PETG into the AMS, slice the plate as TPU, hit Print plate. This is the only way to get the exact UI above. Faking a Bambu device isn't practical — that transport goes through Bambu's proprietary networking plugin (`BBLPrinterAgent` wraps the closed-source DLL), so you can't stand up a stub broker against it.

**A fake FlashForge printer — no hardware, and it exercises real mismatch code.** FlashForge's local API is plain HTTP on port 8898 ([Flashforge.cpp:642](src/slic3r/Utils/Flashforge.cpp#L642)). `fetch_material_slots` POSTs to `/detail` with `{"serialNumber": ..., "checkCode": ...}` and reads `matlStationInfo.slotInfos[]`, taking `slotId`, `hasFilament`, `materialName`, `materialColor` ([Flashforge.cpp:545](src/slic3r/Utils/Flashforge.cpp#L545)). Serve that from a 30-line Python script on localhost, add a physical printer with host type FlashForge pointing at `127.0.0.1` with any serial and check code, and you get `FlashforgePrintHostSendDialog` with its own slot-mapping grid. Its match rule is a normalized string comparison of project material vs. slot material ([PrintHostDialogs.cpp:1047](src/slic3r/GUI/PrintHostDialogs.cpp#L1047)), and auto-selection picks the nearest color among type-matching slots. Report PETG in every slot, slice in TPU, and you'll see it refuse to auto-assign. Different dialog from the Bambu one, same underlying question.

**A fake Moonraker/AFC printer — exercises the ingestion half.** `MoonrakerPrinterAgent::fetch_moonraker_filament_data` GETs `/server/database/item?namespace=lane_data` and reads each lane's `lane`, `material`, `color`, `bed_temp`, `nozzle_temp` ([MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp:730](src/slic3r/Utils/MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp#L730)); if that 404s it falls back to Happy Hare at `/printer/objects/query?mmu`. It also needs `/server/info`, `/printer/objects/list`, and `/printer/objects/query?print_stats&virtual_sdcard&extruder&heater_bed&fan` for the connection to come up. Stubbing those five GETs gets you printer-reported type and color flowing into `DevAmsTray` and out through `build_filament_ams_list()` into the sidebar's filament dropdowns and the "Sync filament from printer" dialog. What you won't get is the send-dialog mapping badge, since that's Bambu-gated. Worth knowing: this Moonraker filament sync is upstream OrcaSlicer, not a fork addition — commits `055f24ca7a` and `189bcafee0`, first tagged in v2.3.2 (2026-03-23) and present in v2.4.0.

**Instrumentation, if you just want the decision trace.** `DevMappingUtil::ams_filament_mapping` already logs a full distance matrix at info level, one row per sliced filament, one column per slot, prefixed `ams_mapping_distance:`. Every 999999 in that grid is a type or alpha mismatch. Turning on verbose logging against a real printer gives you the algorithm's reasoning without touching code.

Sources: [issue #12554](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/issues/12554), [issue #13103](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/issues/13103), [issue #14249](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/issues/14249)

content.text:
**Moonraker/AFC, clearly.** It reaches the same code the Bambu path uses; FlashForge is a separate, smaller implementation.

## The deciding fact

I assumed earlier that the mismatch UI was Bambu-only. That's true of the *send-print-job* dialog, but not of the mapping machinery. `SyncAmsInfoDialog` — the dialog behind the sidebar's "Synchronize filament list from AMS" button — calls the exact same functions:

- `DevMappingUtil::ams_filament_mapping()` at [SyncAmsInfoDialog.cpp:1260](src/slic3r/GUI/SyncAmsInfoDialog.cpp#L1260), so you get the real 999999-on-type-mismatch distance matrix and its `ams_mapping_distance:` log output
- `DevMappingUtil::is_valid_mapping_result()` at [line 1288](src/slic3r/GUI/SyncAmsInfoDialog.cpp#L1288)
- `AmsMapingPopup` at [line 630](src/slic3r/GUI/SyncAmsInfoDialog.cpp#L630) — the same popup class that carries the "Note: the filament type(%s) does not match with the filament type(%s) in the slicing file" text at [AmsMappingPopup.cpp:1586](src/slic3r/GUI/AmsMappingPopup.cpp#L1586)

And that button is explicitly *not* Bambu-gated. [Plater.cpp:2472](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp#L2472) shows it for any non-Bambu printer whose agent reports a filament sync mode other than `none`:

```cpp
// ORCA: show/hide sync-ams button based on filament sync mode
auto agent = wxGetApp().getAgent();
if (agent && agent->get_filament_sync_mode() != FilamentSyncMode::none)
    p->m_bpButton_ams_filament->Show();
```

So a fake Moonraker printer gets you the production mapping algorithm, the production mapping popup, and the production mismatch copy. A fake FlashForge printer gets you none of those — `FlashforgePrintHostSendDialog` is a parallel implementation with its own `slot_matches_filament()`, a plain normalized string equality on material name with color used only to break ties among already-type-matching slots.

## Scenario coverage

Moonraker lets you vary, per lane, entirely from JSON you control: material type, color, bed/nozzle temps, lane index, and presence (`has_filament` is derived as `!tray_type.empty()`, so an empty `material` gives you the checkerboard "?" placeholder state). Lane count drives multi-AMS layout — `ams_count = (max_lane_index + 4) / 4` — so ten lanes gives you three AMS units to map across. There are also two distinct ingestion shapes to exercise: AFC-style `lane_data` and the Happy Hare fallback, which take different code paths into the same tray struct. Because it's pull mode, `build_filament_ams_list()` re-fetches on every sync, so you edit the JSON and click the button again without restarting Orca.

FlashForge gives you four fields per slot — `slotId`, `hasFilament`, `materialName`, `materialColor` — plus the IFS on/off toggle and a multi-material validation error. Real scenarios, but a much smaller matrix, and the behavior you'd be characterizing wouldn't generalize to the Bambu path you actually care about.

## The tradeoff, and one thing I haven't verified

FlashForge is cheaper to stub: one POST to `/detail` on port 8898. Moonraker needs about five endpoints for the device to come up — `/server/info`, `/printer/objects/list`, `/printer/objects/query?print_stats&virtual_sdcard&extruder&heater_bed&fan`, then `/server/database/item?namespace=lane_data` (or `/printer/objects/query?mmu`).

The agent also opens a websocket status stream (`start_status_stream`). I have not verified whether the device reaches connected state with the websocket absent or failing — the HTTP connect path and the WS thread are separate, and the WS has reconnect logic, so I'd expect it to tolerate a missing socket, but that's a hypothesis, not something I confirmed. Budget for possibly having to serve a stub websocket.

Setup detail worth knowing: which agent is active comes from the `printer_agent` string on the selected printer preset ([GUI_App.cpp:3577](src/slic3r/GUI/GUI_App.cpp#L3577)). Only one stock profile sets it to `moonraker` — `resources/profiles/OpenEYE/machine/fdm_openeye_common.json` — so either select an OpenEYE printer or add `"printer_agent": "moonraker"` to a custom printer profile pointed at your stub.

content.text:
Yes — the stub is a standalone process, nothing in the OrcaSlicer tree.

It's just an HTTP server on a port that answers the handful of Moonraker REST paths the agent GETs. A single Python file with `http.server` or FastAPI is enough. OrcaSlicer talks to it the same way it would talk to a real Klipper box: over the network, by host address. No recompile, and you can edit the fake lane JSON and re-click "Synchronize filament list from AMS" while the app stays running, because pull mode re-fetches on every sync.

Two supporting pieces also live outside the repo:

**The printer preset.** The agent is chosen by the `printer_agent` string on the selected printer profile. Selecting the stock OpenEYE profile needs nothing at all. If you'd rather use a different printer model, create a custom printer preset in the UI and set that field — user presets are written to your OrcaSlicer data directory, not the source tree. You'd only touch `resources/profiles/` if you wanted a permanent vendor profile, which testing doesn't need.

**The host address.** `init_device_info` builds the base URL by plain string concatenation — `"http://" + dev_ip` at [MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp:1076](src/slic3r/Utils/MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp#L1076) — with no port appended, and `dev_ip` comes from the MachineObject's stored address ([DeviceManager.cpp:2412](src/slic3r/GUI/DeviceManager.cpp#L2412)). So your stub either listens on port 80, or the address you configure has to carry the port itself. I traced that concatenation but did not follow `get_dev_ip()` all the way back to the field you type in, so I can't promise the connect flow accepts a `host:port` form — worth checking early, since it decides whether you need to run the stub privileged on port 80.

content.text:
No, roughly the same size — and the in-tree route is the better bet, because most of the work is already done.

## What's in that worktree

Branch `jusprin-fake-printer-agent` has uncommitted work: `FakePrinterAgent.hpp` (155 lines) and `FakePrinterAgent.cpp` (389 lines), plus a 4-line diff registering it in `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` and `NetworkAgentFactory.cpp`. It implements `IPrinterAgent` directly and replays a scripted list of `FakePrinterStatusStep` values — gcode state, percent, remaining time, nozzle and bed temperatures — on a background thread.

The important part is *how* it delivers them. `build_push_status_json` composes Bambu-format `{"print": {"command": "push_status", ...}}` and `emit_status` hands it to `on_local_message_fn` / `on_message_fn`, which is exactly the pipe a real Bambu printer's MQTT messages travel down into `MachineObject::parse_json`. It currently populates no filament fields at all — no `ams` block, no `vt_tray`, no `get_filament_sync_mode()` override.

## What adding filament faking costs

You already have the reference implementation: `MoonrakerPrinterAgent::build_ams_payload()` is 117 lines and builds precisely the JSON that `DevFilaSystemParser::ParseV1_0` consumes — an `ams[]` array of units, each with `id`, `info`, and a `tray[]` of `{id, tag_uid, tray_info_idx, tray_type, tray_color, bed_temp, nozzle_temp_max}`, plus `ams_exist_bits` and `tray_exist_bits` masks.

So: a tray struct mirroring `FakePrinterStatusStep`, a `set_ams_scenario()` mirroring `set_scenario()`, that JSON builder, and a one-line `get_filament_sync_mode()` returning `subscription` so the sidebar's sync button appears. Call it 100–150 lines onto a file that already exists and is already in the build.

Against that, an external Moonraker stub is five canned endpoints and possibly a websocket — maybe 80–150 lines of Python. Comparable. But it's a new process you have to launch alongside the app, it can't run inside a Catch2 test, and it still has the unresolved question of whether the connect flow accepts a `host:port` address for a stub not on port 80.

## The tail of `build_ams_payload` is worth reading before you start

It documents preconditions you'd otherwise hit one at a time as mysterious empty dialogs. After parsing, it sets `obj->printer_type` (without it, sync badges silently clear), forces `m_push_count` and `m_full_msg_count` to non-zero and stamps `last_push_time` so `is_info_ready()` passes, sets `DevStorage::HAS_SDCARD_NORMAL` (the code comments that `SelectMachineDialog` otherwise blocks with "No SD card"), and inserts a placeholder `module_vers` entry. Any fake agent needs the same six lines.

## One thing neither route buys you

Both land on `SyncAmsInfoDialog`, not the Bambu send dialog. `GUI_App::switch_printer_agent()` forces `BBL_PRINTER_AGENT_ID` whenever `is_bbl_vendor()` is true and only consults the preset's `printer_agent` field otherwise, so no custom agent can ever be active for a Bambu profile. Since `SyncAmsInfoDialog` calls the same `DevMappingUtil::ams_filament_mapping()` and the same `AmsMapingPopup`, the coverage is equivalent — you just reach it by a different button. If you specifically want `SelectMachineDialog`, that needs a one-line local patch to the `use_bbl_network()` gate, which works from either fake.
